summary: This informational document describes a framework and reference model for the Interface to Network Security Functions (I2NSF). Network security functions are packet-processing engines, such as firewalls, that inspect and optionally modify traffic. The framework describes the major components needed to let security functions be requested and configured through standard interfaces, including in virtualized environments.

eli5.summary: A school has many different guards. This describes one common way to give any guard instructions, no matter which company made the guard.

questions: how to configure network security functions through a standard interface
how does i2nsf work with virtualized security
subtitle: A standard architecture for configuring network security functions through a unified interface

tldr.problem: Network security functions (firewalls, intrusion detection systems) come from many vendors with different configuration interfaces, making it hard to manage and orchestrate security across a network.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8329 defines the I2NSF (Interface to Network Security Functions) framework with three key interfaces: a user-facing interface for expressing security policies, an NSF-facing interface for configuring individual security functions, and a registration interface for vendors to declare what capabilities their functions support.
tldr.outcome: This enables vendors and enterprises to manage security functions in a technology-independent way, whether physical or virtualized, from different providers.

today: RFC 8329 is an Informational RFC defining the I2NSF framework and reference model. It remains the conceptual foundation for subsequent I2NSF standards that define the actual protocols, data models, and policy structures.

sections.title: Network Security Functions and the Need for Standards
sections.content:
A Network Security Function (NSF) is a packet-processing engine that inspects and optionally modifies traffic as it traverses a network. Examples include firewalls, intrusion detection systems (IDS), intrusion prevention systems (IPS), and Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) engines. These functions are critical to network defense.

Historically, each vendor built their security functions with proprietary configuration interfaces. An enterprise deploying functions from multiple vendors faced a management nightmare: different command syntaxes, different policy languages, and no way to express a unified security intent across the infrastructure. As networks moved toward Software-Defined Networking (SDN) and Network Function Virtualization (NFV), where security functions could be virtual and deployed anywhere, the need for standardized control became acute.

The Interface to Network Security Functions (I2NSF) framework addresses this by defining a standard reference model and set of interfaces that any NSF can implement, making security functions interchangeable from a management perspective.
sections.eli5: Firewalls and intrusion detectors are essential security guards. But if each company's guards only understand their own orders, managing them is chaotic. I2NSF defines universal orders any guard can understand.

sections.title: The I2NSF Reference Architecture
sections.content:
I2NSF defines a three-tier architecture. At the top are I2NSF Users—network managers, application owners, enterprise IT administrators, or overlay network management systems. Below them is the I2NSF Controller (part of the Network Operator Management System), which translates high-level security intent into flow-based rules. At the bottom are the actual Network Security Functions, deployed on physical hardware or as virtual instances.

The framework also recognizes Developer Management Systems belonging to security vendors, who register their NSFs' capabilities so the I2NSF Controller can understand what each function can do. This registration interface allows vendors to add new security capabilities without waiting for standards updates.

The architecture is agnostic to:

  • Network topology or where NSFs are deployed
  • The provider or form factor (physical or virtual)
  • Vendor-specific implementation details
  • Control-plane and data-plane specifics

This agnosticism is essential to allow NSFs to evolve and maintain their competitive advantages while still fitting into the standard framework.
sections.eli5: The structure is: managers (users) at the top, a coordinator (controller) in the middle, and guards (NSFs) at the bottom. The coordinator talks to all guards in the same language.

sections.title: The Three Key Interfaces
sections.content:
The I2NSF Consumer-Facing Interface (facing upward) allows users to define and monitor security policies. A user might say "block all traffic to high-value assets except from the corporate network" or "scan email for malware." These are user-level intents, not low-level packet rules. The interface should abstract away the need for users to know exact IP addresses, field names, or vendor-specific syntax.

The I2NSF NSF-Facing Interface (facing downward) is the protocol-level interface to individual NSFs. It expresses flow-based rules using an Event-Condition-Action (ECA) model: when an event occurs, evaluate a condition, and if true, execute an action. For example: "Event: packet arrives; Condition: source is 10.0.0.0/8 AND destination port is 443; Action: allow and log."

The NSF-Facing Interface includes two sub-interfaces: an Operational and Administrative Interface for programming NSF behavior via I2NSF Policy Rules, and a Monitoring Interface for querying NSF state or receiving reports. The monitoring interface may use other protocols like SYSLOG or DOTS.

The I2NSF Registration Interface allows vendors to register what capabilities their NSFs support—what actions they can perform, what packet fields they can match on, what events they can trigger. This enables dynamic capability negotiation without hard-coding vendor-specific features.
sections.eli5: The user interface accepts goals like "block malware." The NSF interface sends exact rules like "if port is 445, drop it." The registration interface lets a vendor say "I can detect malware" so the controller knows.

sections.title: Flow-Based Security Policies
sections.content:
I2NSF policies are built on the Event-Condition-Action paradigm. Each policy rule has three Boolean clauses that evaluate to TRUE or FALSE.

An Event triggers evaluation. Examples include the arrival of a packet, a change in NSF state, user logon or logoff, or a specific time (like 08:00). Events are when the system should consider applying the rule.

A Condition determines if the action should run. Conditions match on packet content (headers, payload), context (session state, user identity, authentication status), or derived data (reputation scores, geographic origin). For instance: "destination port is 80 AND source IP is not in the trusted list."

An Action specifies what happens: allow, deny, rate-limit, redirect, modify the packet, or log. Multiple actions can be combined.

The user-facing layer allows customers to express policies in more abstract terms ("enable Internet access for authenticated users"), while the NSF-facing layer expresses the same policies as concrete packet-matching rules ("if destination port is 80-443 and source identity matches LDAP group X, then allow"). The I2NSF Controller translates between the two.
sections.eli5: A policy says: "When a packet arrives, if it looks like malware, block it." Event = packet arrives, Condition = looks like malware, Action = block.

sections.title: Security Threats and Safeguards
sections.content:
The framework identifies major threats to externally provided NSFs. An attacker could impersonate a legitimate user to access another user's policies or falsify traffic. A legitimate user could abuse their privileges to harm other users' traffic. A malicious user could install malformed policies to exploit NSF vulnerabilities or intercept other users' traffic. A compromised provider could modify NSF software to alter behavior globally. Physical access could allow an attacker to modify or bypass NSF hardware.

I2NSF requires mutual authentication and authorization for all interfaces. The framework recommends AAA (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting) mechanisms and suggests using attestation to detect unauthorized changes to the I2NSF environment. Users and applications accessing I2NSF should be audited and held accountable.

The I2NSF-Controller-to-NSF connection must use secure, trusted transport. For NSFs in external domains, more restrictive security controls apply. Within a single administrative domain, the same security model applies for consistency.

The framework also emphasizes avoiding ossification: standards should not lock NSF developers into narrow categories or limit innovation. NSF interfaces should be extensible, allowing vendors to add proprietary capabilities beyond the standard set while remaining compatible with the standard management layer.
sections.eli5: Since security guards have power, they could betray you. The system requires proof of identity for everyone, logs all actions, and keeps outsiders' commands locked down.
